transcript:
# Day 20, Psychology, History and Human Nature: Loss aversion and the endowment effect (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; Thaler, 1980)

Picture two versions of the same deal. In the first, your manager says you will get a $1,000 bonus, but if the project slips you lose $500 of it. In the second, she says you will get a $500 bonus, and if the project lands on time you get $500 more. The money is identical in both. Most people feel the first version as a threat and the second as an opportunity, and they work differently under each.

That gap is loss aversion. The idea comes from Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, the two psychologists behind the thinking you met on Day 5 (System 1 and System 2) and Day 10 (anchoring and availability). In 1979 they published prospect theory, a model of how people actually choose when outcomes are uncertain. One of its core claims is simple: losses hurt more than equal gains feel good. Not a little more. Across many experiments the pain of losing $100 is roughly twice the pleasure of winning $100. The exact multiplier varies, but something near two shows up again and again.

The second half of today's idea follows from the first. If losing something hurts more than gaining it feels good, then once you own a thing, giving it up registers as a loss. So you value it more simply because it is yours. Richard Thaler named this the endowment effect in 1980. The classic test came in 1990, when Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Thaler handed coffee mugs to half a class and asked them to name a selling price, then asked the other half what they would pay for the same mug. Sellers wanted about twice what buyers offered. Nothing about the mug changed. Only ownership did.

You see this everywhere once you know to look. A homeowner lists above market and refuses good offers because the house feels worth more to him than to anyone else. A unit resists giving up an aircraft or a mission set it has had for years. A customer stays on a card product she barely uses because closing it feels like losing something. Free trials work on the same logic: once the service feels like yours, cancelling feels like a loss.

Now the honest part. Loss aversion is one of the most cited findings in all of psychology, and it has taken real hits. In 2018 David Gal and Derek Rucker published a paper titled, more or less, the loss of loss aversion, arguing the effect is far weaker and more situational than the field admits. For small amounts, people often do not show it at all. Charles Plott and Kathryn Zeiler showed in 2005 that the mug result shrinks or vanishes when subjects are trained on the procedure and understand it, which suggests part of the effect is confusion about the task rather than a deep feature of the mind. John List found that experienced traders at card shows showed little endowment effect, while novices showed a lot. Defenders answer that none of this kills the idea. Large reviews still find loss aversion in most settings, especially for meaningful stakes, and the fact that experience weakens it is itself useful: it tells you the bias can be trained out. The fair summary is that the effect is real, probably smaller than the textbook version, and heavily shaped by context. Treat the number two as a rough guide, not a law.

This reading closes a short arc. Day 5 gave you the fast system that makes snap judgments. Day 10 showed how it anchors on whatever number it saw first. Day 15 showed how it defends what it already believes. Today shows how it defends what it already owns. All four are the same engine. There is also a direct bridge to the game theory track: prospect theory is item 27 there, and when you get to it, you will see how loss framing changes what counts as a credible threat, the subject of Day 18.

Question for the day: what is one thing you are holding onto, at work or at home, mostly because letting go would feel like a loss rather than because it is still the best option?

Optional source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, chapter 26 (Prospect Theory) and chapter 27 (The Endowment Effect).
